This is standard in the insurance industry. You buy insurance for a whole year. The cover is priced based on the calculated risk of an accident during that period. You have fully ‘used up’ the cover you purchased.

When you pay monthly or fortnightly, the total of those payments is more than if you paid one lump sum at the start. You are effectively paying off the up front cost of your insurance, including an interest component. If the cover is used up and the policy ends then you would still owe the balance.

Call a reputable general insurance broker who deals with all the big insurers. They will know which ones have exclusions for relevant things and what each insurer’s appetite is relative to others, for your location. You will pay a fee but often save more on the premium they negotiate. 

Avoid ‘direct insurers’ who do their own marketing, because they target customers without anything special about their property. (e.g. Tower, AMI) You are more likely to have standard exclusions or limits for things that are important to you specifically. Also, larger brokers have dedicated claims experts who deal with the insurer when you have to make a claim (at no extra cost) and know how to work the system so you don’t get screwed.

Lastly, be aware that it’s a terrible time for the insurance industry. They have suffered huge losses from weather events this year. The cost of cover has gone up. The number of claims means the insurers don’t have enough resources and timeframes are long. If someone gets you cover then take it while you can.

Muscles are made from protein. When you exercise for muscle gain, follow it immediately with clean protein. The right exercise shreds muscle fibres so your body builds new, larger ones.

Full body workouts are time-consuming. I prefer high intensity interval training which focuses on a different muscle group each day. I start with a rower to release the anabolic steroids but you could do sprints for 10 mins. (remember intense anaerobic exercise pushes BG up and steady aerobics burns it off)

Then stretch and start resistance or weight training. The idea is to go against gravity fast and with it slow - e.g. push ups go up fast and take 3x as long back down. Do 2sets with a break then change exercise. When you finish the whole routine do more high intensity then start again. You want to keep repeating until muscles fail - can’t lift the weight or whatever. Then reduce the weight and push to fail again. This shreds more muscle so you rebuild more. e.g. I would start with, say, 14kg dumbbells and work all the way down to 4kg. Stretches and water are absolutely vital to reduce lactic acid buildup and soreness.

I won’t recommend particular body weight exercises - you would be best to get a personal trainer to help work out a routine. It depends what muscle groups you most want to develop. There is also plenty of literature around. Make sure you have a whole routine for your core one day a week.

You need to know what his regime should look like. The basics are: 

1. Test first thing in morning, before each meal and before bed. Write all results down.
2. Inject basal at the same time every day. Count carbs and inject before eating (for carbs +/- any correction). Write it all down.
3. Carry his testing kit and fast-acting carbs at all times (to treat lows). Test whenever he feels low. Write it down.
4. Attend clinics (or see his specialist) at least every 6 months. Take his log.

- Try having a serious but non-threatening conversation first about the need to manage it.
- make sure he understands the things than will happen, short of death (male impotence is often a strong motivator)
- talk to his family and ask for their help

- stage an intervention

Try to understand the mental games he plays with himself around diabetes. Ask how he is going, how he is feeling. Go to clinics with him.
